findings.reason: The protected query is direct, conventional, and expert-interview ready. ranked_sales and sale_number expose the seller-specific chronology, ROW_NUMBER states the second-sale operation exactly, the all-user left-join base makes missing-sale behavior visible, and the CASE expression reads as the required yes/no rule. Short aliases remain unambiguous at each join. No material correctness, complexity, or clarity improvement warrants a candidate.

ROW_NUMBER partitions Orders by seller_id and orders each partition by order_date. Because the source guarantees at most one sale per seller per day, sale_number = 2 identifies exactly one second chronological sale when it exists. Joining that row through item_id obtains its brand. Starting from Users preserves every user, including users with zero or one sale; a null or unequal brand yields no, while equality with favorite_brand yields yes. seller_id and 2nd_item_fav_brand match the required output schema.

A table-native Python oracle independently grouped Orders by seller_id, sorted each group by order_date, selected the second row, and resolved its item brand. It agreed with all seven authored results and 3,000 deterministic randomized schema-valid databases generated with seed 1159. A separate SQL control counted each order's earlier same-seller rows instead of using a window; protected, immutable native, and control queries all matched the oracle.

Metadata identifies Premium database problem 1159, MySQL, and the native query entrypoint. Authenticated evidence confirms the Users(user_id, join_date, favorite_brand), Orders(order_id, order_date, item_id, buyer_id, seller_id), and Items(item_id, item_brand) schemas; every primary- and foreign-key relation; the seller rather than buyer role; unique sale dates per seller; all-user output; lowercase yes/no labels; and unrestricted row order.

Protected sql.sql is byte-for-byte identical to immutable leetcode.sql bound to verified submission 2067869186. Both use the same seller-partitioned date ranking, row-two join, item lookup, all-user left-join base, brand comparison, aliases, and deterministic final ordering. Neither SQL source nor submission.json changed during review.

For r total input rows, partitioned window ranking requires at most O(r log r) comparison-based sorting. The subsequent primary-key joins and projection stay within that time bound. Ranking and join state use O(r) working space. These conservative engine-independent bounds meet the Optimal branch manifest.

The unchanged hidden tiers scale one seller from 32 through 128 to 256 sales on unique dates, an 8x span that forces complete seller ranking. The exact protected query passed all seven ordinary cases, all three benchmark outputs, and scaling at a 0.93x largest runtime ratio and -0.05 extra growth exponent. The independently correct predecessor-count control passed every output but failed only scaling at 11.02x and +0.94. benchmark.json required no edit.

The Approach exactly matches seller-partitioned ROW_NUMBER, order_date chronology, row-two filtering, Items attachment, the Users left-join base, and null-safe CASE behavior. It defines r, derives O(r log r) time and O(r) space, and covers correlated lookup, aggregate alternatives, inner-join loss, buyer/seller confusion, order IDs, and missing second sales.

The modular Reference preserves all three source table schemas and types, every primary- and foreign-key fact, the online-marketplace roles, second item by date, fewer-than-two behavior, per-seller date uniqueness, all-user result, exact aliases and labels, unrestricted order, the complete source example, and each of its four user explanations. Its seven Markdown tables are informationally equivalent to the seven logical source tables.

A fresh authenticated Premium review confirmed three schema tables, one explained example containing three input tables and one output table, no constraints, no hints, no notes, no images, and no diagrams. source_fidelity.json binds every modular section to live statement hash 5337d374cca9b956e1ba173173ed43d512ca2cdc63278d159f99d10d03b84e35 and validates without errors.

coverage: sample-1 preserves the only authenticated source example: every Users, Orders, and Items cell; all four output rows; and the explanations that user 1 sold nothing, users 2 and 3 matched their favorite brands on their second sales, and user 4 did not.

All seven ordinary fixtures are visible samples or trials. They cover users with zero and one sale, exactly two and more than two sales, favorite and nonfavorite second brands, an irrelevant favorite first brand, an irrelevant favorite third brand, order_date differing from order_id order, buyer/seller role separation, and same-day sales by different sellers while retaining the one-sale-per-seller-per-day guarantee.

The table-native Python oracle and independent predecessor-count SQL control agreed with every expected result, exact protected bytes, and exact immutable native bytes. Another 3,000 deterministic schema-valid databases generated with seed 1159 varied one through eight users, zero through seven sales per seller, one through ten items, duplicate brands, randomized order IDs and row order, self-purchases, cross-user purchases, positive/negative favorite matches, and unique dates within each seller partition.

The SQL fixture harness infers columns from rows, so a wholly empty Orders fixture is not representable without failing schema creation. Zero-sale behavior is nevertheless proved by the exact source example and the zero/one-sale trial, both of which keep a populated schema-valid Orders table.

The three hidden performance-only tiers keep sales count as size, span 8x from 32 through 256, and isolate ranking versus predecessor-pair growth. Protected passed at -0.05 and 0.93x; the correct quadratic control passed every output and failed only scaling at +0.94 and 11.02x. benchmark.json remained unchanged.
